findings.paper_title: Executive report - Affordable housing acquisitions in Farnham 150926
findings.headline: Property acquisitions transferring to West Surrey Council on 1 April 2027 vesting date during local government reorganisation.
findings.detail: Major property acquisition proceeding before reorganisation vesting date when Waverley merges into West Surrey Council. Council confirms acquisition is necessary and proportionate for continued service delivery through transition. 48 homes and associated HRA borrowing will form part of housing stock and liabilities transferring to successor authority.
findings.matters: Large capital asset acquisition and revenue-generating operations integration during major local government reorganisation presents execution and transition risk; successor council inherits both assets and borrowing obligations.
findings.figures: 48 homes; £14.45m investment; vesting date 1 April 2027
findings.quote: the proposed acquisitions will help meet identified affordable housing need within the borough and will form part of the housing stock transferring to West Surrey Council on 1 April 2027, thereby supporting the delivery of housing services by the successor authority.

findings.paper_title: Executive report - Affordable housing acquisitions in Farnham 150926
findings.headline: Independent viability appraisals confirm schemes fall within Council financial parameters; risks identified around rental income assumptions, maintenance costs, and shared ownership valuations.
findings.detail: Haverly Consulting independently reviewed business cases and viability assessments. Council identifies risks that assumptions (rental income, maintenance costs) may change, to be managed through New Development Impact Reserve. Right to Buy risk flagged: if tenants exercise this before borrowing repaid, retention calculations and Reserve provide protection. Shared ownership valuations to be updated before marketing homes.
findings.matters: HRA taking on long-term revenue exposure; early redemption risk from Right to Buy and valuation shortfall risk on shared ownership sales both affect scheme cash flows and debt servicing.
findings.figures: £14,454,118 budget; 8 shared ownership units at Waverley, 3 at Farnham Oaks create sales-dependent cash flows
findings.quote: There is a risk that some of the assumptions underpinning the business cases and accompanying viability appraisals, including rental income, management costs and maintenance costs, may change over time, adversely affecting the projected net revenue position.

findings.paper_title: Executive report - Affordable housing acquisitions in Farnham 150926
findings.headline: Acquisition subject to West Surrey Shadow Authority Executive consent under Section 24 Direction as capital contract exceeds £1m threshold.
findings.detail: As part of local government reorganisation, West Surrey councils must obtain written consent from shadow authority for contracts exceeding £1m. This acquisition falls outside scope of General Consents granted June 2026. Consent must be obtained before Executive and Council decisions take effect. Timeline: Executive 6 October, Full Council 10 November, then Shadow Executive approval required before completion.
findings.matters: Introduces procedural gate and potential delay risk to project execution during reorganisation period when successor authority must approve major financial commitments.
findings.figures: £14,454,118 exceeds £1m General Consent threshold
findings.quote: The recommendations in this report fall within the scope of the Section 24 Direction but not within the scope of the General Consent, and therefore the Executive and Council is taking the decision subject to the consent of the Shadow Executive being obtained.

findings.paper_title: Executive report - Affordable housing acquisitions in Farnham 150926
findings.headline: Council acquiring 48 affordable homes across two Farnham sites for £14.45m through combination of HRA borrowing and capital receipts.
findings.detail: Waverley Gardens (40 homes: 32 social rent, 8 shared ownership) and Farnham Oaks (8 homes: 5 affordable rent, 3 shared ownership). Acquisition supports Council's housing delivery programme and meets identified local housing need. Independent appraisals confirm financial viability; contingency allowances included in budget.
findings.matters: Large HRA capital investment decision; financing uses HRA borrowing flexibility available after government removed housing investment caps.
findings.figures: £14,454,118 total budget; 40 homes at Waverley Gardens, 8 homes at Farnham Oaks
findings.quote: The acquisitions will be funded through a combination of HRA borrowing and capital receipts, as detailed in Exempt Annex 2.

findings.headline: Service user receivables total £2.36m with 78% more than 90 days overdue, including £474.6k over one year old
findings.detail: Service user and fee payer receivables total £2,355,391. Of this, £1,830,821 is outstanding for more than 90 days, comprising £705,834 in the 90-180 day bracket, £650,372 in the 180-365 day bracket, and £474,615 aged over one year. The current amount (0-90 days) is £524,571.
findings.matters: The aging profile of receivables affects cash flow and liquidity; large overdue balances increase bad debt write-off risk and require provisioning, impacting available resources.

findings.headline: Spend with local suppliers rose significantly to 18% of third-party spend, but remains below a 25% target and within amber tolerance.
findings.detail: New indicator R12 tracks local supplier spend. Q1 performance was 18%, amber-rated against a 25% target and 15% tolerance threshold. The report notes this represents a significant increase from 11% in 2025—a 7-percentage-point jump. Postcodes define 'local' as Waverley and adjacent Guildford postcodes.
findings.matters: Local supplier spend demonstrates procurement social value. Auditors track whether councils meet procurement social value commitments. An upward trend suggests policy traction but not yet at target.
findings.figures: Q1 18% vs target 25%; increased from 11% in 2025; tolerance 15% (red threshold)
findings.quote: Based on the data from the postcodes above, Local Supplier spend has increased significantly. In 2025 overall spend with our local suppliers was 11%, so it has increased by 7%.

findings.headline: Affordable housing delivery totalled 72 units in Q1, with 43 built by the council and 29 by other providers.
findings.detail: The council delivered 43 affordable homes directly (across Ockford Ridge, Bargate Lodge, Pathfield B, Ridgley Road, and Hawthorns) with a further 29 delivered by registered providers (Sovereign, VIVID). Mix includes affordable rent, social rent, and shared ownership tenures.
findings.matters: Affordable housing delivery is a capital programme commitment. Tracking delivery pace matters to lenders and councils monitoring HRA capital capacity and strategic housing objectives.
findings.figures: 72 total affordable homes delivered; 43 council-built; 29 by other providers
findings.quote: A total of 72 affordable homes were delivered in Q1 – 43 were delivered by the Council and another 29 were delivered by other providers.

findings.headline: Homelessness prevention improved to green, with 51.9% of cases (58 households) successfully supported in Q1.
findings.detail: Homelessness prevention recovered from amber to green status. Of 112 households seeking support (52 on prevention duty, 44 on relief duty), 51.9% achieved positive outcomes—58 households total. Relief duty showed stronger success at 70.4% (18 of 44). The service is responding to the improvement trend after Q4 showed deterioration.
findings.matters: Successful homelessness prevention avoids the higher cost of temporary accommodation and reactive support. The shift to green signals improved cost management on a budget pressure that has been growing.
findings.figures: 51.9% success rate (58 of 112 households); prevention duty 51.9% (27 of 52); relief duty 70.4% (18 of 44); target 55%
findings.quote: During Q1 2026/27 51.9% of those who sought homelessness support were successfully supported, representing 58 households.

findings.headline: Tenant satisfaction with housing repairs fell to 79.8% against a 90% target and has not historically achieved that threshold.
findings.detail: Tenant satisfaction with responsive repairs remains below the 90% target at 79.8% for Q1. The report notes this target has not been achieved historically. Performance was volatile within the quarter: 79.1% in April, fell to 74.6% in May, recovered to 85.7% in June. The council is working with contractors on service quality and resident communication.
findings.matters: Persistent tenant dissatisfaction signals service delivery issues in council housing. It carries reputational risk and can impact rent collection and tenant retention, affecting HRA revenue stability and debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: Q1 average 79.8%; April 79.1%, May 74.6%, June 85.7%; target 90%; tolerance 85.5%
findings.quote: Customer satisfaction remains below the current target of 90%, which has not been achieved historically.

findings.headline: Data protection subject access requests breached 100% statutory response target in Q1, with 3 of 14 requests answered late.
findings.detail: Data protection compliance fell to 78.6% (3 of 14 requests missed the statutory deadline), down from 100% target. The report notes requests are complex and time-consuming, requiring collation of hundreds of pages and sensitivity checks. The council has agreed to apply extensions in future for time-consuming requests.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory deadlines on data protection requests creates legal and reputational risk. The ICO can impose fines; councils have a duty to respond within statutory timescales under GDPR.
findings.figures: 14 requests received; 3 responded to outside statutory timeframe; performance 78.6% vs 100% target
findings.quote: In Q1 14 requests were responded to over the quarter, and 3 of these were outside of the statutory timescale, as such we have missed the target of 100% and the KPI is red rated.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation households doubled in one quarter from 6 to 12, a cost pressure on HRA.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation headcount grew from 6 households in Q4 2025-26 to 12 in Q1 2026-27—a doubling. This follows prior growth from 9 in Q4 2024-25 to 6 in Q4 2025-26, showing volatility and current upward pressure. Temporary accommodation is a variable cost charged to revenue.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a costly service: each household in temporary housing generates revenue expenditure. A jump of this magnitude in one quarter flags emerging demand pressure on HRA budgets.
findings.figures: Q4 2025-26: 6 households; Q1 2026-27: 12 households

findings.headline: Council tax collection recovered to target after falling short in the prior quarter, reaching 24.8% cumulative in Q1.
findings.detail: Council tax collection improved from amber status in Q4 2025-26 to green in Q1 2026-27, meeting the cumulative target of 24.8% for the quarter. Business rates collection followed the same trajectory, recovering from red status in Q4 to green in Q1, also hitting the 24.8% target. Both remain the only income metrics actively monitored in the report.
findings.matters: Council tax and business rates are the council's primary revenue sources. Recovery after falling short last quarter signals improved collection performance after prior period weakness.
findings.figures: R3 target 24.8% cumulative (Q1), tolerance 23.6% (red threshold); R4 target 24.8% cumulative (Q1), tolerance 23.6% (red threshold)
findings.quote: Performance in Q1 is within the target set.
